african-bush-elephant.anatomy: An elephant's trunk is a fusion of its nose and upper lip, with no bones, and is used for breathing, smelling, drinking, trumpeting, touching, grabbing and fighting. African elephants have two finger-like tips at the end of the trunk for picking up small objects. The tusks are enormously enlarged incisor teeth that keep growing throughout life; both males and females of the bush elephant usually have them, and they are used for digging, stripping bark and fighting. Behind them, elephants have only four big grinding molars at a time, replaced from the back about six times over a lifetime. Their huge ears are laced with blood vessels, and flapping them cools the blood. Their skin is up to 2.5 centimetres thick in places, wrinkled to hold moisture, and they protect it from sun and insects by spraying themselves with mud and dust.
african-bush-elephant.family: Elephant society is built around females. A herd is a family of related females and their young, led by the oldest matriarch, and several families may meet up in larger groups. Females give birth after a pregnancy of about 22 months, the longest of any land mammal, usually to a single calf weighing around 100 kilograms. The calf can stand within an hour, and the whole family helps care for it: older sisters and aunts, called allomothers, guard, comfort and babysit it. Calves suckle for several years. Young males leave the herd as teenagers and join loose groups of bulls. Adult bulls regularly enter a state called musth, when hormones surge, they become aggressive, and they search widely for females. Elephants grieve: they touch and stand over the bodies of dead relatives and return to their bones.
african-bush-elephant.people: Elephants have been revered, feared and hunted by people for thousands of years. Ivory was carved into art and ornaments across the world, and demand for it drove two great poaching waves, in the 1970s and 1980s and again after 2008, which killed hundreds of thousands of elephants. In 1989 the international ivory trade was banned, and countries including China and the United States have since closed most of their domestic ivory markets. Today, elephants attract millions of tourists to national parks, supporting jobs and conservation funding. As farms spread, conflict grows when elephants raid crops; communities in Kenya and elsewhere use fences hung with beehives, which elephants avoid, and chilli smoke to keep them out. Researchers fit elephants with GPS collars to understand their movements and protect corridors between parks.

cheetah.anatomy: A cheetah is built more like a greyhound than a lion. It has a small, rounded head, a deep chest with large lungs and heart, a narrow waist and long, slender legs. Its spine is unusually flexible, bending and stretching with each stride so that, at full speed, the cheetah covers around 7 metres per stride. Its enlarged nostrils and nasal passages take in plenty of air during a chase. Its short coat is pale gold with solid black spots, and its long tail, spotted near the base and ringed toward the tip, swings to counterbalance sharp turns. The claws only partly retract and are blunt, like running spikes, but a sharp dewclaw on each front leg is used to trip and hold prey. Cheetahs have excellent eyesight, with a band of sensitive cells that lets them scan the horizon.
cheetah.family: Female cheetahs live alone, except when raising cubs. After a pregnancy of about three months, a mother gives birth to around three to five cubs, in a hidden spot in tall grass or thickets. The cubs have a long, silvery mane along their backs that may make them look like honey badgers, fierce animals predators avoid. The mother moves them often to keep them hidden, but lions and hyenas still kill many. At about six weeks, cubs begin following their mother, and she brings them live prey to practise on. They stay with her for around 18 months. After they leave, brothers often stay together for life, forming groups called coalitions that hold territories and hunt together. Sisters soon split up and live on their own.
cheetah.people: Cheetahs have been tamed and used for hunting by royalty in Egypt, Persia and India for thousands of years. Akbar, the 16th-century Mughal emperor of India, is said to have kept a thousand. That history contributed to their decline in Asia; the last cheetahs in India were shot in the 1940s, and from 2022 cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa were brought to India's Kuno National Park in an attempt to bring them back. In Africa, most cheetahs live on farmland, where farmers have shot them to protect livestock. The Cheetah Conservation Fund in Namibia breeds large Anatolian shepherd guard dogs and gives them to farmers; the dogs scare cheetahs away, and farmers are far less likely to kill cheetahs. Cheetah cubs are also smuggled to the Middle East as pets, a trade conservationists are fighting.

okapi.anatomy: An okapi has a dark, velvety, reddish-brown coat that is oily and water-repellent, helping it stay dry in the rainforest. Its legs carry bold horizontal stripes of white and black, and its ankles are white. Like a giraffe, it has a long neck relative to many hoofed animals, although nothing like a giraffe's, and males have two short, skin-covered horns called ossicones. Its tongue is dark and prehensile, around 35 centimetres long, used to strip leaves from branches. Okapis have large ears that pick up quiet sounds, and their sense of hearing and smell are better than their eyesight in the dim forest. They have scent glands on their feet that leave a tar-like mark wherever they walk, helping them mark territories and find one another.
okapi.family: Okapis are solitary and meet only to breed. After a pregnancy of around 14 to 15 months, a female gives birth to a single calf, which can stand within half an hour. Within days the calf goes into a nest in thick vegetation, where it spends most of its first two months hiding, emerging mostly to suckle. During this time it barely needs to relieve itself, which keeps its hiding place free of scent that might attract leopards. Mothers communicate with their calves using very low-frequency sounds, possibly below the range that predators can hear well. The calf is weaned at about six months but stays near its mother for longer. Young okapis develop their full adult size over about three years.
okapi.people: The okapi has always been known to the Mbuti and other peoples of the Ituri Forest. European explorers heard rumours of an 'African unicorn' and of a horse-like animal with stripes, and in 1901 British colonial official Harry Johnston obtained skin and skulls, leading to its scientific description. It was named Okapia johnstoni after him. The okapi became a national symbol of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In 1992, the Okapi Wildlife Reserve was created in the Ituri Forest; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. During years of war and conflict in the region, rangers and conservation staff have faced violence, including a deadly attack on the reserve's headquarters in 2012, in which okapis at the breeding station were also killed. Conservation now includes supporting nearby communities with schools, healthcare and farming help.

bornean-orangutan.anatomy: Bornean orangutans have long, shaggy, reddish-brown hair, very long arms that can span over 2 metres, and short, bowed legs. Their hands and feet are hook-like, with curved fingers and toes that grip branches, and their feet can grasp like hands. Adult males grow to roughly twice the weight of females. Some develop large cheek pads called flanges and a big throat sac; these 'flanged' males dominate others and attract females. Other males may stay 'unflanged' for years, looking more like females, and only develop flanges later, often when a dominant male disappears. Orangutans have excellent colour vision for spotting ripe fruit, and big, powerful jaws and teeth that can crack hard nuts and strip tough bark. They are the heaviest tree-dwelling animals, moving by climbing and swinging rather than jumping.
bornean-orangutan.family: Orangutans are the most solitary of the great apes. Adult males roam alone; females travel with their young. A female gives birth to a single baby after about eight and a half months, and the baby clings to her fur for its first year or more, nursing for up to six or seven years. She carries it through the canopy, teaches it which of hundreds of plants are good to eat, how to build nests, and how to use tools. Young orangutans learn by watching and copying, and different orangutan populations have different traditions, a sign of culture. Because a mother has a baby only every six to eight years, and females first give birth at around 15, an orangutan mother may raise only a few young in her lifetime, which makes populations very slow to recover from losses.
bornean-orangutan.people: Orangutans feature in the folklore of the peoples of Borneo and Sumatra, and their likeness to humans has fascinated people for centuries. In the 1970s, scientist Biruté Galdikas began studying orangutans in Tanjung Puting, Borneo, and later founded Orangutan Foundation International; her decades of research, along with that of others, revealed much of what we know about their lives. Logging, fires and the spread of palm oil and paper plantations have cleared huge areas of Borneo's forests, and orphaned orangutans are taken in by rescue centres, where they spend years at 'forest school' learning skills their mothers would have taught them before release. Shoppers can help by looking for products made with certified sustainable palm oil, and several governments and companies have pledged to stop deforestation in their supply chains.

platypus.anatomy: The platypus has a soft, rubbery, duck-like bill covered with tens of thousands of receptors: some sense touch, others detect the faint electric fields produced by the muscles of prey, letting it hunt in muddy water with its eyes closed. Its body is streamlined and covered in thick, waterproof brown fur, so dense that it traps a layer of air that keeps the platypus warm in cold streams. Its front feet are webbed for swimming, and the webbing folds back when it walks or digs, exposing strong claws. The hind feet steer and act as brakes, and the broad tail stores fat. Males have a hollow spur on each ankle connected to a venom gland, most active in the breeding season. Adults have no teeth; instead, hard pads in the bill grind food, along with gravel scooped up from the riverbed.
platypus.family: Platypuses breed in late winter and spring. After mating in the water, the female digs a long nesting burrow in the riverbank, sometimes many metres long, and blocks the tunnel with soil plugs to guard against floods and predators. She lays one to three small, leathery eggs, about the size of a grape, and curls around them to keep them warm for around ten days. The hatchlings are tiny, hairless and blind. Platypuses have no nipples: milk oozes from patches of skin on the mother's belly, and the babies lap it up. They stay in the burrow for three to four months before emerging to swim and learn to forage. Males play no part in raising young.
platypus.people: Aboriginal Australians have known the platypus for tens of thousands of years, and it appears in their stories; one tells of a platypus born from a duck and a water-rat. When a preserved platypus reached Britain in 1799, naturalist George Shaw reportedly checked for stitches, suspecting a hoax. Scientists argued for decades over whether it really laid eggs, until this was confirmed in 1884. Platypus fur was once hunted for rugs, and hunting was banned in the early 1900s. Today the platypus appears on Australia's 20-cent coin and is a beloved national symbol. Researchers and volunteers survey rivers using environmental DNA, collecting water samples and testing them for traces of platypus genes. Removing old 'opera house' yabby traps, which drown platypuses, and protecting stream banks are key to their future.

kakapo.anatomy: The kākāpō is a large, round, moss-green parrot, mottled with black and yellow so it blends into the forest floor. It has a face framed by fine, whisker-like feathers, like an owl's, which may help it sense its way in the dark. Its name means 'night parrot' in Māori. Its wings are short and its breastbone lacks the deep keel that anchors flight muscles, so it cannot fly, but it is a strong climber and a powerful walker, sometimes travelling several kilometres a night. It stores large amounts of fat, which helps it survive lean times. Kākāpō have a strong, sweet, musty smell, which may help them find each other but also makes them easy for predators like stoats to find. Their sense of smell is unusually good for a bird.
kakapo.family: Kākāpō breed only in years when certain trees, especially rimu, produce a huge crop of fruit, which may happen every two to four years. Males gather at traditional sites called leks, each digging a bowl in the ground and linking bowls with tracks. Night after night for months, they inflate their chests and boom, a deep sound that carries far, followed by a high 'ching'. Females walk long distances to listen and choose a mate, then raise the chicks alone. A female lays one to four eggs in a nest on the ground. She must leave the nest each night to feed, which once exposed eggs and chicks to predators. Chicks grow slowly and stay with their mother for months. Today rangers watch every nest with cameras and sometimes hand-rear chicks.
kakapo.people: For Māori, the kākāpō was hunted for food and its feathers were woven into prized cloaks. After European settlement, introduced cats, rats and stoats devastated the birds, and by the 1970s the kākāpō was feared extinct, until small populations were found in Fiordland and on Stewart Island. All surviving birds were moved to predator-free islands, and the Kākāpō Recovery program, run by the Department of Conservation with Ngāi Tahu, the iwi of the South Island, now cares for each one. Every bird is named, fitted with a transmitter and given health checks, and its genome has been sequenced to help plan matings. A kākāpō called Sirocco, raised by people, became famous after a 2009 video and served as an official 'spokesbird' for New Zealand conservation. In 2020 the kākāpō was voted New Zealand's Bird of the Year, and again in 2008.

emperor-penguin.anatomy: The emperor penguin is the largest penguin, with a black head and back, white belly, and golden-orange patches on the sides of its neck and the lower part of its bill. Its feathers are short, stiff and packed tightly in several layers, with an underlayer of down, creating a windproof, waterproof coat. Beneath them lies a thick layer of fat. To save heat, emperors have small bills and flippers for their size, and blood vessels in their flippers, legs and nose that exchange heat, warming cold blood returning to the body. They can reduce blood flow to their feet to keep them just above freezing. Their bodies are built for diving: solid bones, and the ability to slow their heart rate and redirect blood to vital organs. In water they are fast and agile; on ice they walk upright or slide on their bellies.
emperor-penguin.family: Emperor penguins gather at their breeding colonies in March and April, at the start of the Antarctic autumn, walking as far as 100 kilometres across the sea ice. Pairs find each other using distinctive calls. In May or June, the female lays a single egg and carefully passes it to the male, who tucks it on his feet under a fold of skin called the brood pouch. She returns to the sea to feed, while males incubate through the darkest, coldest months, huddling in tight groups. The egg hatches after about 65 days. If the mother hasn't returned yet, the father feeds the chick a milky secretion from his throat. When she returns, they swap, and the parents take turns making trips to the sea. Chicks gather in groups called crèches and leave the colony in December or January, as the ice breaks up.
emperor-penguin.people: Emperor penguins live in one of the most remote places on Earth, and the first colony was not discovered until 1902, during Robert Falcon Scott's Discovery expedition. In the Antarctic winter of 1911, three members of Scott's later expedition made a gruelling journey through darkness and extreme cold to collect emperor eggs at Cape Crozier, a trip described in Apsley Cherry-Garrard's classic book 'The Worst Journey in the World'. Today scientists monitor emperor colonies using satellite images, spotting the brown stains left by droppings on the ice from space. This technique has revealed new colonies and shown when colonies fail because sea ice breaks up too early. The emperor penguin was celebrated in films such as 'March of the Penguins', and in 2022 the United States listed it as threatened under its Endangered Species Act because of projected sea-ice loss.
